prompt: A file has a missing bracket on line 40. What happens when you run it?
hint: One of the four in the lesson behaves differently from the other three.

choices.text: It runs, and fails only if line 40 is reached
choices.why: That would be true of a `NameError`. A file that will not parse never starts.

choices.text: It runs and the broken line is skipped
choices.why: Nothing is ever skipped; a file either parses or it does not.

choices.text: Nothing runs at all, not even the `print` on line 1
choices.why: A `SyntaxError` happens before execution: the interpreter could not finish reading the file.

choices.text: Lines 1 to 39 run and then it stops
choices.why: That is every OTHER error. This one is raised while the file is being read.

prompt: A traceback is twelve lines long. Which line do you read first?
hint: The order is upside down on purpose.

choices.text: The first one, so you follow the calls in order
choices.why: That is the chain of calls, oldest first, and in a one-file program it says nothing you need.

choices.text: The one with the caret under it
choices.why: That is second: it says WHERE. The last line says what actually happened.

choices.text: Whichever names a file you wrote
choices.why: Useful for narrowing it down, and not the first question.

choices.text: The last one, which names the kind of failure and the complaint
choices.why: The answer is closest to where your eye already is — at the bottom, where you just pressed Enter.

prompt: Why does `python3` reading your file every time cost you less than it sounds?
hint: Think about where a data program spends its seconds.

choices.text: Modern interpreters compile to machine code as they go
choices.why: That is a different implementation of Python, not the one you installed.

choices.text: Most of the time is spent inside libraries that are not written in Python
choices.why: `pandas` and `numpy` are C underneath; your code is the thin layer saying what to do.

choices.text: The interpreter caches the file after the first run
choices.why: A `.pyc` saves the parse, not the work. The arithmetic is still Python’s.

choices.text: Reading a file is fast compared with running it
choices.why: True and beside the point: the cost is the per-operation overhead, not the read.

prompt: The kind of failure raised when you use a word Python has no meaning for: `______Error`
hint: Four letters before the word Error.

prompt: `x = 5` is best read as which of these?
hint: The difference is invisible with numbers and is the whole story with lists.

choices.text: 5 is copied into the memory reserved for `x`
choices.why: Nothing is reserved and nothing is copied.

choices.text: The name `x` now refers to the value 5
choices.why: Values have types; names do not. A name is a label on a value, not a container.

choices.text: The box called `x` now contains 5
choices.why: There is no box. `x = "five"` afterwards is legal and moves the label.

choices.text: A variable of type int called `x` is declared
choices.why: Nothing is declared and nothing has a type but the value itself.

prompt: `if count:` skips a case that `if count is not None:` does not. Which?
hint: One value is both a real answer and a falsy one.

choices.text: `count` being a string
choices.why: A non-empty string is truthy either way.

choices.text: `count` being `0`
choices.why: Zero is falsy, so a real count of nothing is treated as no count at all.

choices.text: `count` being `None`
choices.why: Both skip that one; that is what they agree about.

choices.text: `count` being a negative number
choices.why: Any non-zero number is truthy.

prompt: `int("3.14")` raises. Why is that better than answering `3`?
hint: Think about what a quiet answer would put into your program.

choices.text: Because `float` and `int` are unrelated types
choices.why: `int(float("3.14"))` is two honest steps and works.

choices.text: A conversion that quietly rounded would put a wrong number in with nothing to read
choices.why: The refusal is the feature, and the message quotes what it was given.

choices.text: Because the string has a character that is not a digit
choices.why: So does `"-4"`, which converts fine. The point is the lost fraction.

choices.text: Because rounding is ambiguous between up and down
choices.why: `int()` already has a rule for that — it truncates towards zero.

prompt: `round(0.5)` is `0` and `round(1.5)` is `2`. What is the rule?
hint: It is deliberate, and it is not about floating point.

choices.text: Halves go down, then up, alternating
choices.why: Nothing alternates; `round(2.5)` is also `2`.

choices.text: `round` truncates when the fraction is exactly a half
choices.why: Truncating would make `round(1.5)` equal `1`.

choices.text: `0.5` cannot be represented exactly, so it rounds down
choices.why: `0.5` is exact in binary. `round(2.5)` being `2` is the rule, not the float.

choices.text: Halves go to the even number
choices.why: Banker’s rounding: it stops a long column of halves drifting upwards.

prompt: Print `total` with a thousands separator: `f"{total:______}"`
hint: One character.

prompt: Which collection answers `in` without walking?
hint: One of them stores a value at a position computed from the value itself.

choices.text: A set
choices.why: A hash gives the position directly, whatever the size.

choices.text: A tuple
choices.why: A tuple is a list that cannot change. The walk is the same.

choices.text: A list
choices.why: A list is slots in order; `in` compares until it finds one.

choices.text: All of them, for small sizes
choices.why: Size is exactly what changes the answer.

prompt: Why can a tuple be a dictionary key and a list cannot?
hint: A key has to keep answering the same question for ever.

choices.text: Tuples are faster to compare
choices.why: They are not, and speed is not the rule.

choices.text: A list has no `__eq__`
choices.why: It does, and two equal lists compare equal.

choices.text: A key’s position is computed from its value, and a list changes in place
choices.why: Change the list and the position it was filed under is no longer where it belongs.

choices.text: A list is too large to hash
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it.

prompt: `b = a[:]` where `a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]`, then `b[0].append(9)`. What is `a`?

choices.why: Only the first inner list was touched.

choices.text: A `TypeError`
choices.why: Nothing here is a type error; it is a shallow copy working as documented.
That would need a deep copy, which `[:]` is not.
The outer list is new; the inner lists are the same objects as before.

prompt: `xs[1:3]` gives two items. What makes the exclusive stop worth having?
hint: Think about what you can say about two slices of one list.

choices.text: `len(xs[a:b])` is `b - a`, and `xs[:n] + xs[n:]` is the whole list
choices.why: No overlap and no gap, because the numbers count the gaps rather than the items.

choices.text: It matches the way `range` works
choices.why: True, and it is the same reason rather than a reason of its own.

choices.text: It makes a slice never raise
choices.why: A slice never raises whatever the stop is.

choices.text: It keeps the first item at index 1
choices.why: The first item is at index 0.

prompt: Turn a list of ids into something `in` can answer in one step: `banned = ______(load_ids())`

choices.text: How many values there will be

choices.text: Which values are kept
choices.why: That is the last clause.

choices.text: What is being built

choices.text: Where the values come from

prompt: A loop removes items from the list it is iterating. Nothing raises. Why is that worse than an error?
hint: Think about what a wrong answer looks like from outside.

choices.text: Because the loop runs more slowly
choices.why: It does not, and speed is not the problem.

choices.text: Because it raises later, somewhere else
choices.why: It usually does not raise at all, which is the whole difficulty.

choices.text: Because the list ends up empty
choices.why: It does not; items are skipped, not lost.

choices.text: The answer is wrong and looks ordinary, so nothing points at the line
choices.why: An error names a file and a line; a skipped item names nothing at all.

prompt: `[y for row in grid for y in row]` — in what order do the two `for` clauses read?
hint: It is the opposite of what most people guess.

choices.text: Left to right, exactly as nested `for` statements would be written
choices.why: The outer loop is the first clause, the inner one is the second.

choices.text: The order does not matter here
choices.why: Swap them and the name `row` is undefined.

choices.text: Right to left, like the expression at the front
choices.why: Only the expression is evaluated last; the clauses are in writing order.

choices.text: Inside out, so `row` is the inner loop
choices.why: `row` comes from `grid`, which is the outer one.

prompt: When is `for i in range(len(xs)):` the right thing to write?
hint: There is one honest use and it is narrow.

choices.text: Whenever you need the index
choices.why: `enumerate` gives the index and the item together.

choices.text: When the list is long
choices.why: Length changes nothing about which form to write.

choices.text: When the list might be empty
choices.why: `for item in xs` handles an empty list fine.

choices.text: When you need the position for something other than reading `xs[i]`
choices.why: Otherwise `for item in xs` says it, and `enumerate` gives you both.

prompt: Walk a list and get the position with it: `for i, item in ______(xs):`
hint: Nine letters.

prompt: `total = total + 1` inside a function raises `UnboundLocalError`, and the read looks correct. Why?
hint: The decision is made before a line of the body runs.

choices.text: `+ 1` needs the name to exist first
choices.why: It does, and it would find the global one if the name were not local.

choices.text: The function was called before `total` was set
choices.why: The error is about which scope the name is in, not about timing.

choices.text: The module’s `total` was defined after the function
choices.why: Order of definition is not the rule; the assignment in the body is.

choices.text: An assignment anywhere in the body makes the name local for the whole of it
choices.why: Python scans the body first, so the module’s `total` is never consulted.

prompt: `def add(x, xs=[])` appends to `xs` and returns it. The second call returns two items. Why?
hint: The default is part of the function, not of the call.

choices.text: Lists are passed by reference, so the caller sees the change
choices.why: They are, and that is not this: the surprise is that there is ONE list, not that it is shared.

choices.text: The default list is made once, when the `def` runs
choices.why: Every call that leaves it out gets the same list, which keeps whatever was put in it.

choices.text: `append` returns the list, so it accumulates
choices.why: `append` returns `None`. The accumulation is the shared default.

choices.text: Python caches the return value of a pure function
choices.why: Nothing here is cached and nothing here is pure.

prompt: What does one star mean at a call site, as in `total(*args)`?
hint: It means the same thing in a definition and in a call.

choices.text: Unpack a dictionary into keyword arguments
choices.why: That is two stars.

choices.text: Spread this sequence out into separate positional arguments
choices.why: A definition collects with it; a call scatters with it.

choices.text: Pass the list itself as one argument
choices.why: That is `total(args)`, with no star.

choices.text: Make the arguments optional
choices.why: The star says nothing about optionality.

prompt: Why are `global` and `nonlocal` rare in good code?
hint: Think about what a reader of the signature can tell.

choices.text: They are slower than returning a value
choices.why: Speed is not the objection.

choices.text: They do not work inside a class
choices.why: They do; that is not the reason.

choices.text: A function that changes a name outside itself has an effect its signature does not mention
choices.why: Its result then depends on what ran before it, and a test has to set the world up and put it back.

choices.text: They were deprecated in Python 3
choices.why: Neither has been deprecated.

prompt: Inside a nested function, rebind the name of the function AROUND it: `______ n`

prompt: `ada.school = "another"` on an instance whose class has `school = "codeschool"`. What is `Student.school` afterwards?
hint: Reading and writing do not take the same route.

choices.text: `"codeschool"`
choices.why: Writing always lands on the instance; it made an instance attribute that shadows the class one.

choices.text: An `AttributeError`, because the class attribute is now shadowed
choices.why: The class attribute is untouched and still readable through the class.

choices.text: `"another"` for every instance made after that assignment
choices.why: Nothing about the class changed, so nothing about later instances changed.

choices.text: `"another"`, because the instance reached through to the class it belongs to

prompt: A subclass defines `__init__` and never calls `super().__init__(...)`. What breaks?
hint: Think about what the parent was going to do.

choices.text: The subclass cannot be instantiated at all
choices.why: It can; it just produces a half-built object.

choices.text: Python calls the parent’s `__init__` for you anyway
choices.why: It does not — defining one replaces it entirely.

choices.text: The class loses every method the parent had
choices.why: Methods are found by the lookup chain and are all still there.

choices.text: The parent’s attributes are never set
choices.why: The object is incomplete before your own first line runs, and every method the parent has fails on it.

prompt: A `Notifier` needs to retry on the SMS transport and not on the log one. Which design has somewhere to put that?
hint: Ask whether retrying is a kind of notification.

choices.text: Inheritance, with a `retry` flag on the base class
choices.why: The base then knows about a subclass it is not supposed to know about.

choices.text: Composition — a transport that wraps another transport
choices.why: Retrying happens AROUND a notification rather than being a kind of one.

choices.text: Inheritance, with a `RetryingSmsNotifier` subclass
choices.why: That multiplies a class per combination, and the next requirement doubles it again.

choices.text: Either — the two are the same thing written differently
choices.why: They differ exactly here, which is what makes the question worth asking.

prompt: What does `@dataclass(frozen=True)` give you?
hint: Two things, and the second follows from the first.

choices.text: A copy of the object on every attribute access
choices.why: Nothing is copied; assignment is simply refused.

choices.text: Assignment to a field raises, and the class gets a `__hash__`
choices.why: Something that cannot change can be a dictionary key, which is the point of the pair.

choices.text: Thread safety for every method on the class
choices.why: Frozen fields are not a concurrency guarantee about anything else.

choices.text: A class whose fields are read-only and comparable by identity
choices.why: They are compared by VALUE; that is what `__eq__` is generated for.

prompt: Call the version above this one in the chain: `______().greet()`
hint: Five letters.

prompt: A file called `random.py` sits beside your script. `random.choice(...)` raises `AttributeError`. What happened?
hint: An import walks a list and stops at the first match.

choices.text: `choice` was removed from `random` in this version
choices.why: It was not, and `random.__file__` settles that in five seconds.

choices.text: A stale `__pycache__` shadowed the real module
choices.why: A stale `.pyc` can outlive a deleted file, and here the file is still there.

choices.text: Your file was imported instead of the standard library one
choices.why: The first entry on the path is the script’s own directory, and the error is telling the truth about the wrong file.

choices.text: The standard library module failed to load and was replaced

prompt: What is `if __name__ == "__main__":` for?
hint: It is about one file having two uses.

choices.text: So one file is both a program you run and a module you import
choices.why: Running sets `__name__` to `"__main__"`; importing sets it to the module’s name.

choices.text: Style — every script is expected to have one
choices.why: It is not ceremony: without it, importing runs the program.

choices.text: To mark the entry point for the interpreter
choices.why: The interpreter runs the file you name; nothing looks for a mark.

choices.text: To stop the module running twice
choices.why: Nothing runs twice without it.

prompt: Which of these belongs in `__init__.py`?
hint: It runs when the package is first imported.

choices.text: A re-export and a version string
choices.why: Anything longer is work happening at import, which is the previous section’s problem one level up.

choices.text: A list of the modules the package contains

choices.text: The package’s main logic, so importing it is enough
choices.why: Work at import time is a cost every caller pays and nobody asked for.

choices.text: Nothing at all — an empty file is the only correct one
choices.why: Empty is the clearest default and a re-export is an honest use.

prompt: Why does `pathlib` exist when `os.path` already did?

choices.text: `pathlib` is faster on large directory trees

choices.text: A path becomes an object, so joining and reading are methods rather than functions

choices.text: `os.path` was removed in Python 3

prompt: The name of the file that makes a directory a package: `______.py`

prompt: `except LookupError` catches which of these?

choices.text: A `KeyError` and an `IndexError`

choices.text: Checking is more lines of code

choices.text: Exceptions are cheaper than a function call

choices.text: `os.path.exists` is unreliable on network drives

choices.text: Performance, because a `try` has a cost per statement
